title: String Quartet No. 12 in F major, “American”
hook: Written in about two weeks during a happy summer in a Czech village in Iowa.

painting.title: Canal Scene
painting.collection: Terra Foundation for American Art, Chicago
painting.pairingNote: A sunny canal lock in the American countryside, painted in 1893, the summer Dvořák spent in Iowa; plain colours and open air, like the quartet.

facts: Dvořák spent the summer of 1893 in Spillville, Iowa, a village of Czech immigrants that his secretary Josef Kovařík came from. He arrived in early June and wrote to a friend how happy the family was there, away from busy New York.
He sketched the quartet in three days and finished it in thirteen more, writing at the end “Thank God! I am content. It was fast.” It came just after the *New World* Symphony.
He wanted, he said, to write something “very melodious and straightforward”, with “dear Papa Haydn” before his eyes. The four players often play simple tunes over simple accompaniments.
Almost every theme uses the [[pentatonic-scale|pentatonic scale]], five notes instead of seven. It gives the music its open, folk-like sound, though Dvořák used it in Czech-flavoured music too.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a viola’s open-air song (I), a lament in the minor (II), a quick dance with a bird calling overhead (III), a chugging, train-like finale (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro ma non troppo
movements.summary: The violins set up a soft, rippling shimmer and the viola, usually the quietest voice in a quartet, sings the first theme. It is a cheerful [[sonata-form|sonata form]] movement with a gentler second tune, a busier middle and a bright ending.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, open-air
mainIdeas.description: a simple, rising tune on the viola, built on five notes.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, tender
mainIdeas.description: a gentler melody for the first violin, decorated with little turns.

stops.hear: The violins ripple softly on one unchanging chord; the viola enters with a cheerful, rising tune
The first violin takes the tune up high; the music begins to move to new chords
stops.happening: The theme passes to the violin

stops.hear: A gentler, lyrical melody on the first violin, decorated with little turns
The rippling and the viola tune return
Darker and busier; short pieces of the themes are passed around, and at the end the instruments come in one after another with the same tune
The opening tune returns, then the cello sings alone for a moment
stops.happening: The [[recapitulation|recapitulation]]; the cello bridges to Theme 2

stops.label: Last 40 seconds
stops.hear: Quick, bright and loud, all four players together

notice: In the first seconds, listen to the chord under the viola. It does not change for a dozen bars, which gives the opening its calm, open feel.
Sing the viola’s tune back to yourself and count its notes. There are only five different ones.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The Pavel Haas Quartet, from Prague, recorded the quartet in the Rudolfinum in June 2010, and the disc was named the Gramophone Recording of the Year in 2011. On the Spotify album Quartet No. 13 comes first; the *American* is tracks 5–8.

movements.heading: Lento
movements.summary: A slow, aching song in D minor. The first violin sings it over a soft, pulsing accompaniment; the cello repeats it. A more urgent middle section rises and falls, and at the end the cello sings the song again over the thinnest of accompaniments.

mainIdeas.name: The lament
mainIdeas.description: a long, sad melody built on the same five-note scale, now in the minor.

mainIdeas.name: The pulse
mainIdeas.description: second violin and viola rocking gently underneath.

stops.hear: A soft, rocking pulse in second violin and viola; then the first violin sings a long, sad melody
stops.happening: The main theme. Some have linked it to an African American spiritual or a Kickapoo tune; neither link is proven

stops.hear: The cello takes the melody, deep and warm
The music becomes more urgent; pieces of the melody climb and swell
The cello sings the melody again over a thin accompaniment, part bowed and part plucked

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The music fades away

notice: Compare the violin and the cello in the first minutes. It is the same melody; in the cello it sounds older and darker.

movements.heading: Molto vivace
movements.summary: A short, quick dance full of off-beat accents. High above, the first violin imitates a bird Dvořák heard in Iowa. The dance alternates twice with a slower, smoother version of itself in the minor.

mainIdeas.name: The dance
mainIdeas.description: a bouncing, slightly lopsided tune, with accents in unexpected places.

mainIdeas.name: The bird
mainIdeas.description: a short, insistent call high in the first violin.

stops.hear: A loud, bouncing tune in second violin and cello together, full of off-beat accents
A short, chattering call high up on the first violin
stops.happening: Dvořák’s birdsong. He thought it was a scarlet tanager; it was probably a red-eyed vireo

stops.hear: The music slows to half speed and turns smooth and sad, in the minor
stops.happening: The dance tune transformed, in F minor

stops.hear: The bouncing dance returns, bird call and all
The minor version again, now with a pulsing, three-to-a-beat accompaniment
The dance one last time

notice: Listen for the bird. It interrupts the dance from above, as if it did not care about the rhythm below.

movements.heading: Finale: Vivace ma non troppo
movements.summary: A cheerful [[rondo|rondo]]: one main tune keeps coming back between contrasting episodes. Underneath, the second violin and viola keep up a steady chugging rhythm that many hear as a train, one of Dvořák’s passions.

mainIdeas.name: The chug
mainIdeas.description: a steady, repeated rhythm in second violin and viola.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo tune
mainIdeas.description: a bright, skipping melody on the first violin, five notes again.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: a quiet, slow, [[chorale|chorale]]-like episode in the middle.

stops.hear: Second violin and viola start a steady chugging rhythm; the first violin tries out fragments
The first violin plays the bright, skipping main tune
A more lyrical tune, in a new key
The main tune returns
Everything slows and softens; the four players move together like a quiet hymn
The chugging and the main tune come back
The lyrical tune again

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The main tune, faster and louder, to a bright final chord

notice: Keep your ear on the second violin and viola. Their chugging rhythm hardly stops, and once you hear it as a train it is hard to unhear.

threads.title: Five notes
threads.body: The [[pentatonic-scale|pentatonic scale]] runs through all four movements and gives the quartet its open, simple sound.

threads.title: Every voice has a turn
threads.body: The viola opens the first movement, the cello sings the Lento, and the inner voices drive the finale.

threads.title: America through Czech ears
threads.body: Written in America and named after it, but the critic Paul Griffiths argued that the only American thing about it is where it was written.

threads.title: Haydn’s simplicity
threads.body: Dvořák aimed for clear tunes and clear forms, and said that thinking of Haydn made it all turn out simply.
